a2-perfekt-haben.title: Perfekt Tense: Talking About the Past with Haben
a2-perfekt-haben.pattern: haben (conjugated) + Partizip II (ge- + stem + -t/-en, sent to the end)
a2-perfekt-haben.explanation: The Perfekt is the everyday past tense in spoken German — far more common than any simple past form. Most verbs form it with a conjugated form of "haben" plus a past participle (Partizip II), which is pushed to the very end of the sentence: "Ich habe gestern gearbeitet" (I worked yesterday). Regular participles add "ge-" and "-t": machen → gemacht, spielen → gespielt.
a2-perfekt-haben.fact: Verbs ending in -ieren (often borrowed from French/Latin, like "studieren", "telefonieren") drop the "ge-" prefix entirely in their participle: "studiert", "telefoniert" — not "gestudiert". This is a small but very reliable exception worth memorizing as its own rule.

dialogue.native: Ich habe einen Film gesehen und mit Freunden telefoniert.
dialogue.en: I watched a movie and talked on the phone with friends.

a2-perfekt-sein.title: Perfekt with Sein: Movement and Change Verbs
a2-perfekt-sein.pattern: sein (conjugated) + Partizip II, for verbs of movement/change of state
a2-perfekt-sein.explanation: About a dozen verbs — mostly involving movement from one place to another, or a change of state — use "sein" instead of "haben" in the Perfekt: "gehen" (to go) → "ich bin gegangen", "fahren" (to drive/go) → "ich bin gefahren", "kommen" (to come) → "ich bin gekommen", "werden" (to become) → "ich bin geworden", "bleiben" (to stay) → "ich bin geblieben", "aufstehen" (to get up) → "ich bin aufgestanden".
a2-perfekt-sein.fact: A helpful way to remember which verbs take "sein": they almost always describe moving FROM one place/state TO another (gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen, aufstehen) or a fundamental change (werden, sterben, wachsen) — plus the two exceptions "sein" and "bleiben" themselves, which don't fit the movement pattern but still take "sein".

dialogue.native: Bist du gestern ins Kino gegangen?
dialogue.en: Did you go to the movies yesterday?

a2-dativ.title: Dativ: The Indirect Object Case
a2-dativ.pattern: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, die (pl.) → den + -n · ein → einem, eine → einer
a2-dativ.explanation: The Dativ case marks the indirect object — typically the person receiving or benefiting from something. All three genders change: "der" → "dem", "die" → "der", "das" → "dem", and the plural "die" → "den" (with an extra "-n" added to the noun itself if it doesn't already end in one): "Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch" (I give the man the book). Indefinite articles follow the same pattern: "ein" → "einem", "eine" → "einer".
a2-dativ.fact: A handful of common prepositions ALWAYS take the Dativ: "mit" (with), "nach" (after/to), "aus" (from/out of), "bei" (at/near), "seit" (since), "von" (from/of), "zu" (to) — often memorized together as "mit nach aus bei seit von zu", the Dativ counterpart to Akkusativ's "für durch ohne gegen um".

a2-wechselpraepositionen.title: Wechselpräpositionen: Two-Way Prepositions
a2-wechselpraepositionen.explanation: Nine common prepositions can take EITHER Akkusativ or Dativ, depending on meaning: use Akkusativ for movement TOWARD a destination (answering "wohin?"), and Dativ for a static location (answering "wo?"). "Ich gehe in die Küche" (I'm going into the kitchen — Akkusativ, movement) versus "Ich bin in der Küche" (I am in the kitchen — Dativ, location). The nine: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen.
a2-wechselpraepositionen.fact: A simple test: if the sentence describes crossing a boundary or arriving somewhere (usually with a motion verb like gehen, legen, stellen, setzen), use Akkusativ. If it describes something already positioned or happening in place (usually with sein, liegen, stehen, sitzen), use Dativ.

dialogue.en: It's lying on the sofa, but it's about to jump onto the table.

a2-possessive-separable.title: Possessive Articles Across Cases, and Separable Verbs
a2-possessive-separable.pattern: mein/dein/sein/ihr/unser/euer/ihr + case endings · separable prefix moves to the end
a2-possessive-separable.explanation: Possessive articles (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr/Ihr) take the SAME case endings as "ein": "mein Bruder" (Nom.), "meinen Bruder" (Akk.), "meinem Bruder" (Dat.). Separately, many German verbs have a separable prefix that detaches and moves to the very end of the sentence in the present tense: "aufstehen" (to get up) → "Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf" (I get up at seven o'clock) — the prefix "auf-" jumps to the end.
a2-possessive-separable.fact: In the Perfekt tense, the separable prefix reattaches to the participle, with "ge-" inserted BETWEEN the prefix and the stem: "aufstehen" → "aufgestanden" (not "geaufgestanden"), "einkaufen" → "eingekauft" — the prefix always stays glued to the front once the sentence isn't in simple present tense.

dialogue.en: When do you normally get up?

dialogue.native: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf und rufe dann meine Schwester an.
dialogue.en: I get up at six and then call my sister.

a2-reflexive.title: Reflexive Verbs: Actions Done to Oneself
a2-reflexive.explanation: Reflexive verbs need a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject: "ich freue mich" (I am happy, literally "I please myself"), "du freust dich", "er/sie/es freut sich", "wir freuen uns", "ihr freut euch", "sie freuen sich". Many everyday routine verbs are reflexive in German even when their English translation isn't: "sich anziehen" (to get dressed), "sich waschen" (to wash up).
a2-reflexive.fact: Some reflexive verbs take a Dativ reflexive pronoun instead of Akkusativ when there's already a direct object in the sentence: "Ich wasche mich" (Akkusativ — I wash myself) but "Ich wasche mir die Hände" (Dativ — I wash my hands, literally "I wash to-myself the hands") — the Dativ "mir" appears because "die Hände" is already the direct object.

dialogue.native: Freust du dich auf das Wochenende?

dialogue.en: Yes, I'm very much looking forward to it! I like relaxing at home.

a2-comparatives.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparatives.explanation: Comparatives add "-er" to the adjective, followed by "als" (than): "Sie ist größer als ich" (She is taller than me). Superlatives use "am" plus the adjective with an "-sten" ending: "Er ist am größten" (He is the tallest). Many short, common adjectives also add an umlaut in both forms: "groß" → "größer" → "am größten", "alt" → "älter" → "am ältesten".
a2-comparatives.fact: "Gut" (good), "viel" (much), and "gern" (gladly) have completely irregular comparative/superlative forms, just like English "good/better/best": "gut" → "besser" → "am besten", "viel" → "mehr" → "am meisten", "gern" → "lieber" → "am liebsten" (a very common way to say what you like best: "Ich trinke am liebsten Tee" — I like drinking tea best).

dialogue.native: Dieses Restaurant ist besser als das andere, oder?
dialogue.en: This restaurant is better than the other one, right?

dialogue.native: Ja, und es ist das beste im ganzen Viertel, finde ich.
dialogue.en: Yes, and I think it's the best in the whole neighborhood.

a2-imperative.title: Imperative: Giving Commands
a2-imperative.pattern: du-form: stem (no -st) · ihr-form: present tense minus pronoun · Sie-form: infinitive + Sie
a2-imperative.explanation: The du-imperative drops "-st" from the regular present-tense stem: "du gehst" → "Geh!" (Go!). The ihr-imperative is identical to the ihr present-tense form, just without the pronoun: "ihr geht" → "Geht!". The formal Sie-imperative simply inverts the infinitive and "Sie": "Gehen Sie!" (Go!, formal). Verbs with a stem vowel change (e→i/ie) keep that change in the du-form: "du sprichst" → "Sprich!", "du liest" → "Lies!".
a2-imperative.fact: "Sein" has a genuinely irregular imperative that doesn't follow any of these patterns: "Sei ruhig!" (Be quiet!, du), "Seid ruhig!" (ihr), "Seien Sie ruhig!" (Sie) — these forms must simply be memorized.

items.de: Ich hoffe, wir können sie bald besuchen, auch wenn es nur für ein paar Tage ist.
items.en: I hope we can visit her soon, even if just for a few days.

items.de: Klar, sie ist die Freundin, mit der ich im Leben am meisten geteilt habe.
items.en: Of course, she's the friend I've shared the most with in life.

items.de: Wir haben viel in diesem Level behandelt, und du hast enorme Fortschritte gemacht.
items.en: We've covered a lot at this level, and you've progressed enormously.

items.de: Ich hoffe, du übst weiter alles, was du gelernt hast.
items.en: I hope you keep practicing everything you've learned.

items.de: Die Person, die diesen Kurs begonnen hat, ist nicht dieselbe wie die, die ihn heute beendet.
items.en: The person who started this course isn't the same one finishing it today.

items.de: Ich bin sicher, dass du bereit für das nächste Level bist.
items.en: I'm sure you're ready for the next level.
